exercises.prompt: An upper stage has a specific impulse of 350 s and burns from 40 t to 10 t. What velocity change does it give, in m/s, to the nearest 10 m/s? (Take $g_0 = 9.80665$ m/s².)

feedback.message: Not yet: the rocket equation uses the natural logarithm of the mass ratio, not the ratio itself: $\ln 4 = 1.386$.
Not yet: that uses $\log_{10}$. The rocket equation needs the natural logarithm.

exercises.solution:
The exhaust speed is $v_e = 350 \times 9.80665 = 3432$ m/s, and

$$\Delta v = v_e \ln\frac{m_0}{m_f} = 3432 \times \ln 4 = 3432 \times 1.3863 = 4758\ \text{m/s} \approx \mathbf{4760\ m/s}.$$

Three-quarters of this stage's mass is propellant, yet it provides only about half of the 9.4 km/s needed for orbit. The logarithm is why rockets are mostly propellant and why every kilogram of landing gear and reserve propellant on a reusable stage costs payload.

exercises.prompt: A first stage with a dry mass of 25 t (including legs and fins) must keep enough propellant to give itself 1.2 km/s for its entry and landing burns, with an average specific impulse of 300 s. How many tonnes of propellant must it hold in reserve? Give the nearest whole number.

feedback.message: Not yet: that is roughly the linearised estimate $m\,\Delta v/v_e$. The rocket equation is exponential: the reserve must also decelerate itself.
Not yet: that is the total mass at the start of the burns. Subtract the 25 t dry mass to get the propellant.

hints: Rearrange the rocket equation: $m_0/m_f = e^{\Delta v / v_e}$, with $m_f$ the dry mass.
exercises.solution:
With $m_f = 25$ t and $v_e = 2942$ m/s,

$$m_0 = m_f\,e^{\Delta v/v_e} = 25\,e^{1200/2942} = 25 \times 1.504 = 37.6\ \text{t},$$

so the reserve is $37.6 - 25 = 12.6 \approx \mathbf{13\ t}$ of propellant, which the stage cannot use on the way up. In the lesson's model this, with 2 t of recovery hardware, cost 11% of the payload. A return to the launch site needs about 3 km/s and roughly 48 t in reserve.

exercises.prompt: Why did the lesson's booster land softly under closed-loop guidance planned for 80% throttle, but not under an open-loop full-thrust burn with the same half-second timing error?

options.label: Because the closed-loop burn used more propellant.
options.feedback: Not yet. It used a little more than the ideal full-thrust burn, but propellant alone does not correct a timing error; the ability to change thrust does.

options.label: Because planning at 80% leaves throttle margin both ways, and feedback adjusts thrust continuously to the actual height and speed.
options.feedback: Yes. A late start is met by throttling up and an early one by throttling down; at full thrust there is no margin left to throttle up.

options.label: Because closed-loop guidance lets the booster hover until it is ready to land.
options.feedback: Not yet. Even at its deepest throttle, the booster's thrust exceeds its weight, so it cannot hover under any guidance law.

options.label: Because drag was included in the closed-loop simulation.
options.feedback: Not yet. Both simulations ignore drag during the burn.

hints: At full thrust, what can the controller do if the booster is lower than planned?
What is the thrust-to-weight ratio at the deepest throttle?
exercises.solution: **(b).** An open-loop burn at full thrust has exactly one correct ignition height and no way to correct an error: late means too little height to stop, early means stopping in mid-air with thrust still exceeding weight. Planning the burn at 80% leaves authority to throttle between 50% and 100%, and the guidance law recomputes, every instant, the thrust that would stop the booster exactly at the pad. The same principle (plan with margin, then feed back on the measured state) runs through all of control engineering; real landing guidance adds three dimensions, wind and constraints, and solves an optimisation on board.

exercises.prompt: Write `radiator(Q_hot, Q_cold, eps, T_hot_C, T_cold_C, q_hot, q_cold)` returning `(area, heater_W)`. The area is set by the hot case: `Q_hot` watts of electronics must be rejected at `T_hot_C` while the radiator absorbs `q_hot` W/m² from the environment. In the cold case (`Q_cold` watts, `q_cold` W/m² absorbed), return the heater power needed to hold the radiator at `T_cold_C`, or 0.0 if no heater is needed. Use $\sigma = 5.670 \times 10^{-8}$ W/(m²·K⁴).
exercises.tests:
A, heater = radiator(600, 300, 0.85, 20, 0, 150, 60)
assert abs(A - 2.9136) < 1e-3 and abs(heater - 306.9) < 0.5, "the lesson's example"
A, heater = radiator(1000, 800, 0.9, 30, -10, 120, 50)
assert abs(A - 3.2157) < 1e-3 and heater == 0.0, "the cold-case power keeps it warm enough"
A, heater = radiator(400, 350, 0.8, 25, -20, 100, 40)
assert abs(A - 1.5478) < 1e-3 and heater == 0.0
hints: Hot case balance per square metre: emitted $\varepsilon\sigma T^4$ minus absorbed $q$ equals $Q/A$.
So $A = Q_\text{hot}/(\varepsilon\sigma T_\text{hot}^4 - q_\text{hot})$, with temperatures in kelvin.
Cold case: heater $= A(\varepsilon\sigma T_\text{cold}^4 - q_\text{cold}) - Q_\text{cold}$, but never negative.
exercises.solution:
```python
SIGMA = 5.670e-8

def radiator(Q_hot, Q_cold, eps, T_hot_C, T_cold_C, q_hot, q_cold):
    T_hot, T_cold = T_hot_C + 273.15, T_cold_C + 273.15
    area = Q_hot / (eps * SIGMA * T_hot**4 - q_hot)
    heater = area * (eps * SIGMA * T_cold**4 - q_cold) - Q_cold
    return area, max(0.0, heater)
```

For the lesson's spacecraft the radiator needs 2.91 m² and about 307 W of heater power in the cold case. In the other two cases the cold-case dissipation is a large fraction of the hot-case power, so the spacecraft stays above its minimum without heaters. That is the design lever: keep the power swing between hot and cold cases small, or make the radiator's effective area variable with louvres or variable-conductance heat pipes.

exercises.prompt: A fusion magnet's conductor sits in a field of 13 T. What is the magnetic pressure $B^2/2\mu_0$ on it, in MPa, to the nearest whole number? ($\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ H/m.)

feedback.message: Not yet: you have $B^2/\mu_0$. The magnetic pressure has a factor of 2 in the denominator.
Not yet: square the field: $13^2 = 169$ T².

exercises.solution:
$$p = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0} = \frac{169}{2 \times 4\pi \times 10^{-7}} = 6.72 \times 10^7\ \text{Pa} \approx \mathbf{67\ MPa},$$

about 660 atmospheres, acting continuously while the magnet is on and cycling each time it is energised. Because pressure rises with $B^2$, the higher fields that high-temperature superconductors allow come with much larger forces, so the steel structure, not the superconductor, often sets the size and mass of a compact fusion magnet.

exercises.prompt: A D–T fusion device produces 500 MW of fusion power, but only for a quarter of the year on average. Each reaction releases 17.6 MeV and consumes one tritium nucleus (3.016 u). How many kilograms of tritium does it burn in a year? Give the nearest whole number.

feedback.message: Not yet: 56 kg is for a full gigawatt running all year. Scale by 0.5 for the power and 0.25 for the time.
Not yet: you have scaled for the power but not for running only a quarter of the year.

hints: Each reaction releases $17.6 \times 1.602 \times 10^{-13}$ J; each consumes $3.016 \times 1.661 \times 10^{-27}$ kg of tritium.
exercises.solution:
Energy released in a year: $5 \times 10^8 \times 0.25 \times 3.156 \times 10^7 = 3.94 \times 10^{15}$ J. Each reaction releases $17.6\ \text{MeV} = 2.82 \times 10^{-12}$ J, so there are $1.40 \times 10^{27}$ reactions, each consuming $5.01 \times 10^{-27}$ kg of tritium:

$$m = 1.40 \times 10^{27} \times 5.01 \times 10^{-27}\ \text{kg} \approx \mathbf{14\ kg}.$$

Equivalently, a quarter of the lesson's 56 kg per gigawatt-year. Even an experimental machine running a fraction of the time would need a large share of the world's civilian tritium stock of a few tens of kilograms, which is why breeding blankets are on the critical path.

exercises.prompt:
Using the lesson's plant model, net electric power is

$$P_\text{net} = \eta_\text{th}\,(g_b P_\text{fus} + P_h) - \frac{P_h}{\eta_h} - P_\text{other}, \qquad P_h = \frac{P_\text{fus}}{Q}.$$

Write `q_needed(P_fus, heat_eff=0.40, blanket_gain=1.15, thermal_eff=0.35, other=60.0)` returning the smallest plasma gain $Q$ for which $P_\text{net} > 0$ (the break-even value), or `None` if no gain, however large, gives net electricity.
exercises.starter:
def q_needed(P_fus, heat_eff=0.40, blanket_gain=1.15, thermal_eff=0.35, other=60.0):
    raise NotImplementedError
exercises.tests:
assert abs(q_needed(500.0) - 7.6106) < 1e-3, "the lesson's 500 MW plant"
assert abs(q_needed(2000.0) - 5.7718) < 1e-3, "a bigger plant needs less gain"
assert q_needed(100.0) is None, "too small: the plant's own loads exceed what even infinite Q can deliver"
assert abs(q_needed(500.0, thermal_eff=0.45) - 5.1572) < 1e-3, "better thermal efficiency helps"
hints: Substitute $P_h = P_\text{fus}/Q$ and collect terms: $P_\text{net} = (\eta_\text{th} g_b P_\text{fus} - P_\text{other}) - P_h(1/\eta_h - \eta_\text{th})$.
If $\eta_\text{th} g_b P_\text{fus} \le P_\text{other}$, even infinite $Q$ (no heating at all) cannot give net power.
exercises.solution:
Collecting terms, $P_\text{net} = (\eta_\text{th} g_b P_\text{fus} - P_\text{other}) - P_h(1/\eta_h - \eta_\text{th})$. The first bracket is the most the plant could ever deliver (with no heating); the second term is the net cost of heating. Setting $P_\text{net} = 0$:

$$Q_\text{min} = \frac{P_\text{fus}(1/\eta_h - \eta_\text{th})}{\eta_\text{th} g_b P_\text{fus} - P_\text{other}}.$$

```python
def q_needed(P_fus, heat_eff=0.40, blanket_gain=1.15, thermal_eff=0.35, other=60.0):
    surplus = thermal_eff * blanket_gain * P_fus - other
    if surplus <= 0:
        return None
    return P_fus * (1 / heat_eff - thermal_eff) / surplus
```

The 500 MW plant breaks even at $Q \approx 7.6$, a 2 GW plant at 5.8, and a 100 MW plant never, because its fixed loads exceed what its blanket could convert. Break-even is not a business, though: a commercial plant needs most of its gross output to be sellable, which pushes designs to $Q$ of 20–30 or more and to large fusion powers.

exercises.prompt: Which statements about fusion gain are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: NIF's December 2022 shot released more fusion energy than the laser energy delivered to the target.
options.feedback: Yes: 3.15 MJ out for 2.05 MJ of laser light in, a target gain of about 1.5.

options.label: NIF's December 2022 shot released more fusion energy than the facility drew from the electricity grid.
options.feedback: Not yet. The lasers drew roughly 300 MJ from the grid, about a hundred times the fusion yield.

options.label: A magnetic-confinement plant with plasma gain Q = 1 would consume far more electricity than it produced.
options.feedback: Yes. Heating systems, conversion losses and the plant's own loads mean Q = 1 loses hundreds of megawatts in the lesson's model.

options.label: ITER is designed to reach Q = 10 and to supply electricity to the French grid.
options.feedback: Not yet. ITER aims at Q = 10, but it has no turbines or generators; it is an experiment, not a power plant.

options.label: Engineering gain compares the electricity a plant exports with the electricity it consumes.
options.feedback: Yes. It is the figure that matters for a power plant, and it needs plasma or target gain far above 1.

hints: Distinguish the energy delivered to the fuel from the energy drawn from the wall plug.
Does ITER have a turbine hall?
exercises.solution: **(a), (c) and (e).** Scientific (plasma or target) gain compares fusion energy with the heating energy that reaches the fuel; engineering gain compares electricity out with electricity in. NIF crossed the first threshold in 2022 but is about a hundredfold short of the second, because of the inefficiency of its lasers. A magnetic-confinement plant similarly needs Q well above 1 just to cover its heating systems and other loads (the lesson's model needs about 7.6 to break even at 500 MW). ITER aims at Q = 10 but generates no electricity (d is false); demonstration power plants such as Europe's planned DEMO are meant to take that step.
